good: PR #2291 moves where we store user login sessions, from Redis to Postgres. Why: under heavy traffic, Redis was dropping sessions and logging people out (incident INC-114). Sessions now live in a new sessions table, added by migration 0087. A new setting, SESSION_TTL_HOURS, controls how long a login lasts (default 72 hours). For the next 7 days, existing logins are still read from Redis, so nobody is signed out by the switch. What to watch: when that 7-day fallback ends, check for a spike in unexpected logouts. Link: https://github.com/acme/api/pull/2291
hard_fail: PR #2291 moves user login sessions from Redis to Postgres. Why: under heavy traffic, Redis was evicting session keys to free memory, which logged people out mid-session; this was the root cause of incident INC-114. Sessions are now stored in a new sessions table, created by migration 0087, so they survive memory pressure the way any other database row does. The PR also adds a new environment variable, SESSION_TTL_HOURS, which sets how long a login stays valid; it defaults to 72 hours, so teams that need a different value should set it before deploy. To avoid a mass sign-out on release day, the code still reads old Redis keys as a fallback for 7 days. Changes touch auth/session.py, settings.py, the migration and tests/test_session.py (+412 / -96). What to watch: unexpected logouts when the fallback window closes, and extra load on the primary database. Link: https://github.com/acme/api/pull/2291
weak_quality: PR #2291 moves user sessions from Redis to Postgres. Why: Redis evictions were logging users out under load (incident INC-114). Migration 0087 creates a new sessions table and copies every existing Redis session into it, so the cutover happens in one step. A new SESSION_TTL_HOURS setting controls how long a login lasts and defaults to 24 hours. What to watch: users may be asked to sign in again more often after deploy. Link: https://github.com/acme/api/pull/2291
